items.title: Normal monomorphisms and conormal epimorphisms
The kernel of a monomorphism is zero and the cokernel of an epimorphism is zero
items.strategy: Use the universal properties of kernel and cokernel against the unique maps to and from a zero object. Monicity or epicity forces every candidate factorization through the zero map.

items.title: The cokernel of the zero map out of the zero object is the target, and dually for kernels
items.strategy: Check that the identity of the target satisfies the cokernel universal property of the zero map out of the zero object, and dualize for kernels into the zero object.

items.title: Image and coimage in a category with kernels and cokernels
A morphism factors uniquely through its coimage
items.strategy: Apply the cokernel universal property to the kernel of the morphism, since the composite with that kernel is zero.

items.title: A morphism factors uniquely through its image
items.strategy: Apply the kernel universal property to the cokernel of the morphism, since the composite with that cokernel is zero.

items.title: The canonical morphism from the coimage to the image exists and is unique
items.strategy: Compose the two universal factorizations of the same morphism. Uniqueness on one side identifies the mediating arrow uniquely.

items.title: The coimage projection is epic and the image inclusion is monic
items.strategy: The coimage map is a cokernel and the image map is a kernel, so the standard equalizer and coequalizer calculus applies directly.

items.title: Abelian category
This page uses Grothendieck's AB1 and AB2 labels, and records the competing conventions
An abelian category is balanced
items.strategy: For a bimorphism, compute the coimage and image using the zero kernel and zero cokernel, identify both endpoint objects, and use the AB2 isomorphism between coimage and image.

items.title: The opposite of an abelian category is abelian
items.strategy: Passing to the opposite preserves additivity, swaps kernels with cokernels and swaps image with coimage, so the same AB2 clause is carried to itself.

items.title: Every monomorphism is the kernel of its cokernel, and dually every epimorphism is the cokernel of its kernel
items.strategy: For a monomorphism, the kernel is zero, so the coimage is the source. AB2 identifies that source with the image, which by definition is the kernel of the cokernel.

items.title: Every morphism factors as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism, uniquely up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Take the canonical coimage to image map, use AB2 to make it an isomorphism, and compose it with the epic coimage projection and monic image inclusion. Uniqueness follows from balancedness applied to the comparison map between two epi-mono factorizations.

items.title: The image is the least subobject through which a morphism factors
items.strategy: Use the epi-mono factorization and compare any other factorization through a subobject to the image factorization by the universal property of the kernel of the cokernel.

items.title: In an abelian category, monic means zero kernel and epic means zero cokernel
items.strategy: An abelian category is preadditive with a zero object, so the published kernel and cokernel characterizations apply immediately.

items.title: Freyd's axioms A0, A1, A1*, A2, A2*, A3, and A3* for abelian categories
Freyd's axioms force the additive structure and recover the AB2 definition
items.strategy: First prove balancedness directly from normality and conormality, then show the canonical map from coproduct to product is an isomorphism, recover the unique commutative-monoid enrichment from biproducts, and use the shear automorphism on a biproduct to build additive inverses.

items.title: Freyd and Mitchell's characterisation of abelian categories
items.strategy: Compare the working AB2 formulation with the Freyd normal-conormal axiomatisation. The equivalence runs by recovering additivity from Freyd's axioms, using the published finite-limit and finite-colimit theorem for the pullback and pushout clause, and recovering products, coproducts, kernels, and cokernels from pullbacks and pushouts against the zero object.

items.title: Additivity can be derived rather than postulated, depending on the axiomatisation
An abelian category has all finite limits and all finite colimits
items.strategy: The ambient category is additive and has kernels and cokernels, so the published finite-limit and finite-colimit theorem for additive categories applies directly.

items.title: A pullback is the kernel of the difference of the two legs, and dually for pushouts
items.strategy: On a biproduct, package the two legs into a single map to the codomain. Equalizing the two composites is equivalent to killing their difference, so the pullback is realized as that kernel.

items.title: The pullback of an epimorphism is an epimorphism
items.strategy: Write the pullback as a kernel inside a biproduct and use exactness of the resulting short sequence to identify the pullback projection as a cokernel-zero map.

items.title: The pushout of a monomorphism is a monomorphism
items.strategy: Dualize the pullback-of-epimorphisms theorem through the opposite abelian category.

items.title: In a pullback square, the induced map on the kernels of the two parallel arrows is an isomorphism
items.strategy: Use the pullback-as-kernel description together with the universal property of kernels to build inverse comparison maps between the two kernels.

items.title: A square with monic legs is a pullback exactly when it identifies the source with the intersection subobject
items.strategy: Interpret the two monics as subobjects of the common codomain, identify their pullback with the greatest lower bound, and compare the induced map from the source to that intersection.

items.title: Pullback pasting in an abelian category
items.strategy: Cite the published pullback-and-pushout pasting theorem and record that it applies verbatim in abelian categories.

items.title: Kernel and cokernel are mutually inverse order-reversing correspondences between subobjects and quotient objects
items.strategy: Send a subobject to the cokernel of a monic representative and a quotient to the kernel of an epic representative. Normality and conormality show the two constructions undo one another, and factorization reverses the order.

items.title: The quotient of an object by a subobject
The quotient by a subobject is independent of the chosen representing monomorphism
items.strategy: Mutually factoring monic representatives have canonically isomorphic cokernels, so the quotient depends only on the subobject class.

items.title: First isomorphism theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: The quotient by the kernel is the coimage, the image is the kernel of the cokernel, and AB2 identifies the two through the canonical coimage-to-image morphism.

items.title: Third isomorphism theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Apply the first isomorphism theorem to the canonical quotient map between successive quotients and identify its kernel with the intermediate quotient subobject.

items.title: The quotient by the kernel followed by the image inclusion is the canonical epi-mono factorization
items.strategy: Compare the quotient-by-kernel factorization from the first isomorphism theorem with the canonical image factorization and use uniqueness of epi-mono factorizations.

items.title: Exact functor between abelian categories
A left or right exact functor between abelian categories is automatically additive
items.strategy: One-sided exactness preserves the relevant finite limits or colimits, hence zero objects and biproducts. The published biproduct-preservation criterion then forces additivity.

items.title: Left exactness, right exactness, and exactness are characterized by short exact sequences
items.strategy: Once one-sided exactness is known to imply additivity, the short exact sequence tests are equivalent to preserving finite limits or finite colimits in the abelian setting.

items.title: An additive functor is exact exactly when it preserves kernels and cokernels
items.strategy: Use the published kernel criterion for left exactness and its opposite-category dual for cokernels, then combine both halves with the definition of exactness.

items.title: A left exact functor preserves monomorphisms and a right exact functor preserves epimorphisms
items.strategy: Translate monicity and epicity into zero-kernel and zero-cokernel conditions, then apply the short-exact-sequence characterization of one-sided exactness.

items.title: An exact functor need not be faithful
items.strategy: Take the product of two nonzero abelian categories and verify its abelian structure componentwise: preadditivity, zero objects, kernels, cokernels, biproducts, and the coimage-image comparison all reduce to the factors. Projection to the first factor therefore preserves kernels and cokernels and is exact, but it sends every morphism supported in the second factor to zero, so it is not faithful.

items.title: An equivalence between abelian categories is exact
items.strategy: Equivalences preserve and reflect all limits and colimits that exist, so they preserve finite biproducts, kernels, and cokernels. The published biproduct-preservation criterion then gives additivity, and the left- and right-exact clauses follow from the preserved finite limits and colimits.

items.title: Abelian subcategory and exact embedding
Abelian groups form an abelian category
items.strategy: Identify abelian groups with $\mathbb Z$-modules. Ordinary subgroup kernels and quotient cokernels give the categorical kernel and cokernel constructions, biproducts are direct sums, and the first isomorphism theorem identifies coimage with image, verifying the abelian-category axioms directly.

items.title: Modules over a ring form an abelian category
items.strategy: Use the ordinary module kernel and cokernel constructions, note that the category is additive and complete enough, and recognize AB2 as the first isomorphism theorem for modules.

items.title: Additive functors from a small preadditive category to an abelian category form an abelian category
items.strategy: The additive-functor category is already preadditive. Kernels, cokernels, biproducts, and the coimage-image map are computed pointwise in the ambient functor category, so the abelian structure descends pointwise as well.

items.title: A small product of abelian categories is abelian
items.strategy: All structure is computed componentwise: preadditivity, zero objects, kernels, cokernels, biproducts, and the AB2 map all reduce to the corresponding statements in each factor.

items.title: Filtered vector spaces can be additive with kernels and cokernels without being abelian
items.strategy: Use the standard one-dimensional filtered-vector-space witness in which the identity map has trivial kernel and cokernel but is not an isomorphism because the filtrations differ.

items.title: Torsion-free abelian groups do not form an abelian category
items.strategy: In the torsion-free full subcategory of abelian groups, multiplication by 2 on Z is monic and epic by cancellation but not invertible. That shows balancedness fails, so the subcategory cannot be abelian.

items.title: An abelian category that is a preorder is trivial
items.strategy: In a preorder every morphism is both monic and epic, so balancedness forces every morphism to be an isomorphism. A preorder with a zero object and only isomorphisms collapses to the trivial case.

items.title: Freyd-Mitchell gives a fully faithful exact embedding of every small abelian category into a module category
The library does not use Freyd-Mitchell to prove the diagram lemmas
FALSE: every additive category with all kernels and cokernels is abelian
items.strategy: Refute with the filtered-vector-space example, where kernels and cokernels exist but the canonical coimage-to-image morphism can fail to be an isomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: if coimage and image happen to be isomorphic as objects, then the canonical map is automatically an isomorphism
items.strategy: Refute with multiplication by 2 on Z inside torsion-free abelian groups: coimage and image are both Z, but the canonical map is multiplication by 2 rather than an isomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: in an abelian category a morphism can be monic and epic without being an isomorphism
items.strategy: Balancedness is precisely the theorem that rules this out.

items.title: FALSE: every abelian category is equivalent to a module category
items.strategy: Refute with finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field: they form an abelian category, but they do not have the countable coproducts that every module category has.

items.title: FALSE: pullbacks preserve epimorphisms in every category with pullbacks
items.strategy: Refute in the category of Hausdorff spaces: the dense inclusion \(\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R\) is epic because continuous maps into Hausdorff codomains are determined on dense subsets, but its pullback along the inclusion of an irrational singleton is the empty map to a point, which is not epic.

items.title: Kernels, cokernels, images, and coimages in abelian groups are the familiar subgroup and quotient constructions
items.strategy: Compute everything for a homomorphism of abelian groups exactly as in elementary algebra and compare the canonical coimage-to-image map with the usual first isomorphism theorem map.

items.title: A module homomorphism factors as quotient by its kernel followed by inclusion of its image
items.strategy: Use the ordinary module quotient M/ker f and the image submodule im f, then identify their comparison map with the published first isomorphism theorem for modules.

items.title: A pullback of module maps is computed as a kernel of a difference map
items.strategy: For module maps to a common codomain, realize the fibre product as the submodule of pairs whose images agree, then identify that submodule with the kernel of (f,-g).

items.title: Vector spaces over a field form an abelian category
items.strategy: Treat vector spaces as modules over a field and inherit the entire abelian-category structure from the module theorem.

items.title: Representations of the quiver 1 -> 2 in abelian groups form an abelian category
items.strategy: Identify a representation with a homomorphism A -> B in abelian groups and a morphism of representations with a commuting square. Kernels and cokernels are then computed pointwise.

items.title: Topological abelian groups are additive but not abelian
items.strategy: Use continuous homomorphisms as morphisms, note that products, coproducts, and hom-set addition are available, and then exhibit a continuous bijection whose image/coimage comparison fails because the inverse is not continuous in the ambient topological category.

items.title: The third isomorphism theorem in abelian groups matches the categorical statement
items.strategy: Compute (A/C)/(B/C) and A/B explicitly for nested subgroups C <= B <= A and compare them through the ordinary quotient-group map.

items.title: Localization of modules gives an exact functor between module categories
items.strategy: View localization as a functor from R-Mod to S^{-1}R-Mod and use the published exactness of localization to show that it preserves short exact sequences.

items.title: Filtered vector spaces can have zero kernel and zero cokernel without satisfying AB2
items.strategy: Unpack the standard one-dimensional filtered-vector-space witness and compute its coimage, image, and comparison map explicitly.
